followUps:
You cache GraphQL mostly below or beside the HTTP layer, because every query is a POST to one URL. Options: (1) persisted queries sent as GET with a hash, so CDNs can cache by URL; (2) a client-side normalized cache keyed by type and id (Apollo, Relay); (3) server-side caches per resolver or per entity with a DataLoader; (4) cache hints (@cacheControl maxAge) so the response gets the lowest max-age of its fields.

Example: a query mixing a product (max-age 300) and the viewer's cart (max-age 0, private) can only be cached for 0 seconds as a whole, so split public and private data into separate queries.

gRPC is harder to balance because it keeps one long-lived HTTP/2 connection and multiplexes many requests on it, so a connection-level (L4) load balancer sends all of them to one server.

With REST over HTTP/1.1, clients open many short connections, and each new connection can land on a different backend, so traffic spreads naturally. A gRPC client with 1 connection and 1,000 req/s pins all 1,000 on one pod while the others sit idle.

Fixes: an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 (Envoy, a mesh sidecar) balancing per request; client-side balancing with a service-discovery list (round robin over resolved addresses); or periodic connection recycling (max connection age) so clients re-balance.

Yes, it is still idempotent, because idempotent means the server state is the same after one or many calls, not that the response is the same.

First DELETE /items/7 returns 204 and removes the item; the second returns 404 because it is already gone. In both cases item 7 does not exist afterwards. Some APIs return 204 both times to make retries simpler for clients, which is a nice choice but not required. What would break idempotency is a side effect such as writing an audit counter that increases on every call.

Yes, a PATCH can be idempotent, but the HTTP standard does not promise it, so you have to design it that way.

PATCH /users/1 {"name":"Ann"} sets a value, so repeating it gives the same state: idempotent. PATCH /accounts/1 {"op":"add","amount":10} or a JSON Patch that appends to an array changes the state on every call: not idempotent. Starting balance 100 gives 110 after one call and 120 after two.

To make a relative PATCH retry-safe, send an Idempotency-Key or use a conditional request with If-Match and an ETag, so a second attempt against the new version is rejected.

You scale to 1M WebSockets by spreading connections across many cheap, stateless-ish gateway nodes and routing messages between them through a pub/sub layer.

  • Each node holds roughly 50k to 100k idle connections (tune file descriptor limits, kernel buffers, memory about 10 to 50 KB per socket), so 1M needs about 10 to 20 nodes plus headroom.
  • An L4 load balancer spreads new connections; there is no sticky routing needed.
  • A registry (Redis) maps user id to node; Redis pub/sub or Kafka delivers a message to the node that owns the user.
  • Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, otherwise a node restart causes a reconnect storm.

Give every event an increasing id, and let the browser tell the server the last id it saw; the server replays everything after it.

The server sends id: 1042 with each event. When the connection drops, EventSource reconnects automatically and sends the header Last-Event-ID: 1042. The server then reads events 1043 and above from a short-lived buffer (a Redis stream or a Kafka offset) and continues the live feed.

The buffer must be long enough to cover typical outages, say 5 minutes. If the id is too old, send a special event telling the client to refetch full state. Ids must be monotonic per stream.

An API gateway is the single entry point for client traffic into your system, while a service mesh manages the traffic between services inside it.

The gateway handles north-south traffic (outside to inside): public TLS, API keys, quotas, routing by path. The mesh (Istio, Linkerd) uses sidecar or node proxies for east-west traffic: mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts, load balancing and per-hop metrics, without changing app code.

They are complementary. A request passes the gateway once, then every internal call goes through the mesh. A small system often needs only a gateway; the mesh pays off with dozens of services.

You avoid a single point of failure by running many identical gateway instances behind redundant load balancing, and keeping the gateway nearly stateless.

  • At least 3 instances across 2 or more zones, autoscaled, behind a managed L4 load balancer or anycast DNS.
  • Keep state (rate-limit counters, sessions) in a shared store, and decide a fail-open or fail-closed mode if that store is down.
  • Deploy configuration gradually with canaries, because a bad config pushed everywhere is the most common cause of a gateway outage.
  • Use health checks, timeouts and circuit breakers so one slow backend cannot exhaust gateway threads.

code.title: Token bucket: burst, rejection, Retry-After
code.python:
# Token bucket with simulated time (no sleeping), so the output is repeatable.
class Bucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, rate):
        self.cap = capacity      # b: largest burst
        self.rate = rate         # r: tokens added per second
        self.tokens = capacity   # start full
        self.last = 0.0

    def allow(self, now, cost=1):
        # Lazy refill: add what accrued since the last call, capped at b
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True, 0.0
        # Retry-After = time until enough tokens exist
        return False, (cost - self.tokens) / self.rate

b = Bucket(capacity=5, rate=2)   # 2 req/s sustained, bursts of 5
print("capacity=5 rate=2/s")
# O(1) time and O(1) space per key: just two numbers
for t in [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 5.0]:
    ok, wait = b.allow(t)
    print("t=%.1f %s retry_after=%.2fs" % (t, "ALLOW" if ok else "429  ", wait))

followUps:
A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity, while a leaky bucket forces output at a smooth, constant rate.

Token bucket: with capacity 5 and rate 2/s, five requests can pass instantly after a quiet period. Leaky bucket (as a queue): requests enter a queue of size 5 and are processed at exactly 2 per second; the sixth waiting request is dropped, and the downstream never sees a burst.

Pick token bucket to protect an API while keeping clients happy; pick leaky bucket to shape traffic toward a fragile downstream such as a payment provider or a legacy database.

Do the refill, check and decrement inside one Lua script, because Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands, which makes it atomic.

local t = redis.call('TIME')            -- server clock
local s = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
-- refill: min(cap, tokens + (now-ts)*rate)
-- if tokens >= cost: tokens -= cost, allow
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ttl)

Two fields per key, one round trip per request. Use Redis server time, not client time, to avoid clock skew, and set a TTL of about capacity divided by rate so idle keys vanish.

code.title: Fixed window vs sliding log vs sliding counter

followUps:
The sliding window counter can be off by up to roughly the size of the previous window's unevenness, but in practice real traffic gives an error of only a few percent.

It assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly. Limit 100 per 60 s: if all 100 of the previous window came in its last second and we are 30 s into the new window, the estimate counts 100 x 0.5 = 50, but the true count in the last 60 s is 100. So the worst case lets through up to about 2x the limit; the opposite skew can wrongly block.

Cloudflare measured under 1% wrong decisions on real traffic. If you need exactness, use the sliding log.

It depends on what you want to limit: if you count only accepted requests, do not log the rejected ones.

Logging only accepted requests means an abusive client that keeps hammering recovers as soon as the oldest accepted entry ages out: limit 5 per 10 s means it can again do 5 requests after the oldest expires. If you log rejected ones too, a client that keeps retrying stays blocked for as long as it keeps trying, which is a stronger punishment and good for login attempts.

The cost is memory: rejected entries can make the log grow without bound under attack, so cap its length.

For multiple regions, you choose between one global count and independent per-region limits, and most systems accept approximate global limits.

  • Per-region quotas: split 1000/min as 600 and 400 by traffic. Fast and local; a flood in one region only hits that region's share.
  • Asynchronous sync: regions replicate counters about once a second; low latency, with overshoot bounded by sync delay times request rate.
  • Home region per key: route each key to one region; exact, but adds a cross-region round trip.

Use local limits for abuse protection and a home region or reconciled counts for billing quotas.

Token leasing makes the limit slightly looser: the system can exceed the limit by at most the tokens that are leased out and not yet reported.

Example: limit 1000/min, 10 nodes each lease 50 tokens at a time. Up to 10 x 50 = 500 tokens are in local hands, but they are already taken from the shared count, so the total is still bounded by 1000 per window. The real inaccuracy is that a node may hold unused tokens while another node's clients are rejected, so users can see a rejection at 90% usage.

Smaller leases mean better accuracy but more Redis calls; adaptive lease sizes (bigger for hot keys) balance the two.

code.title: Offset duplicates a row, keyset cursor does not
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE posts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO posts VALUES(?,?)", [(i, "post%d" % i) for i in range(1, 11)])

def ids(rows):
    return [r[0] for r in rows]

# Page 1 (newest first), page size 3
page1 = db.execute("SELECT id FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3").fetchall()
print("page 1:", ids(page1))
cursor = page1[-1][0]                    # keyset cursor = last id seen

# A new post arrives while the reader is on page 1
db.execute("INSERT INTO posts VALUES(11, 'post11')")

# OFFSET: skips 3 rows, but the new row pushed old ones down -> duplicate
off = db.execute("SELECT id FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3").fetchall()
print("offset page 2:", ids(off), "(8 repeated)")

# KEYSET: WHERE id < cursor uses the primary-key index, no rows skipped or repeated
key = db.execute("SELECT id FROM posts WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3",
                 (cursor,)).fetchall()
print("keyset page 2:", ids(key))
# OFFSET cost grows with the offset (O(offset)); keyset stays O(page size + log N)

followUps:
Across shards you cannot use a global offset, so you ask every shard for its top N by the sort key and merge the results.

For a page of 20 with a cursor (ts, id): query each of the 4 shards with WHERE (ts,id) < cursor ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, merge the 80 rows in memory, keep the top 20, and return a cursor holding the last (ts, id). Cost is shards x page size per page, not offset. With offset it would be worse: for page 50 each shard has to return its first 1,000 rows. When possible, route by a key so one shard answers the whole query.

Jumping to a date works naturally with keyset pagination because the date becomes the cursor value, so you do not have to count rows from the beginning.

For "jump to 2024-03-01", run WHERE created_at <= '2024-03-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 on an index over (created_at, id); it uses an index seek, costing O(log N + 20). The response then carries a normal cursor for the next page.

You cannot jump to "page 37" cheaply, since the position of a row is not known without counting. Offer date, alphabet or search jumps instead, and approximate totals.

code.title: Idempotency key: replay, mismatch, in-progress
code.python:
import hashlib, json

store = {}          # (account, key) -> record; a unique key in a real DB
charges = []        # the side effect we must not duplicate

def fingerprint(body):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

def pay(account, key, body, crash=False):
    k = (account, key)
    fp = fingerprint(body)
    rec = store.get(k)
    if rec:
        if rec["fp"] != fp:
            return 422, "key reused with different request"
        if rec["state"] == "IN_PROGRESS":
            return 409, "request still in progress"
        return rec["status"], rec["resp"] + " (replayed)"
    store[k] = {"fp": fp, "state": "IN_PROGRESS"}   # atomic insert in real life
    if crash:                                       # server dies mid-request
        return 500, "crash"
    charges.append(body["amount"])                  # the real charge
    store[k].update(state="COMPLETED", status=200, resp="charged %d" % body["amount"])
    return 200, store[k]["resp"]

print(pay("acc1", "k-1", {"amount": 50}))              # first try
print(pay("acc1", "k-1", {"amount": 50}))              # retry: stored response
print(pay("acc1", "k-1", {"amount": 99}))              # same key, new body
print(pay("acc1", "k-2", {"amount": 70}, crash=True))  # crash after insert
print(pay("acc1", "k-2", {"amount": 70}))              # duplicate while IN_PROGRESS
print("total charges made:", charges)

followUps:
The key must come from the client because only the client knows whether two requests are the same logical payment or two different ones.

If the server made the key, a client that times out never received it, so its retry would have no key and would be treated as a new payment: double charge. A client-made UUID is created before the first attempt and reused on every retry, so the server recognises the repeat. The same client is also the one who can safely decide to start a genuinely new payment by creating a new key.

Store it in the main database, in the same transaction as the business write; use Redis only for a fast lock or an extra cache layer.

With the key row in the same database, "charge recorded" and "key completed" commit together or not at all, so after a crash you never have a charge without a key or a key without a charge. A unique index on (account, key) gives you an atomic insert for free. Redis can lose data on failover, and that would let a retry charge twice.

Add a TTL of about 24 hours by purging old rows, and keep the stored response so replays return the same result.

code.title: Dedupe table makes at-least-once exactly-once in effect
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE balance(acc TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amt INTEGER)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE processed(event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY)")  # dedupe table
db.execute("INSERT INTO balance VALUES('A', 100)")

def handle(event):
    # Dedupe row and side effect commit together, in ONE transaction
    try:
        with db:
            db.execute("INSERT INTO processed VALUES(?)", (event["id"],))
            db.execute("UPDATE balance SET amt = amt + ? WHERE acc = ?",
                       (event["amt"], event["acc"]))
        return "applied"
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:        # id seen before -> skip
        return "duplicate ignored"

# At-least-once delivery: e2 arrives twice because its ack was lost
stream = [{"id": "e1", "acc": "A", "amt": 10},
          {"id": "e2", "acc": "A", "amt": 25},
          {"id": "e2", "acc": "A", "amt": 25},
          {"id": "e3", "acc": "A", "amt": -5}]
for e in stream:
    print(e["id"], e["amt"], "->", handle(e))
print("balance:", db.execute("SELECT amt FROM balance").fetchone()[0], "(expected 130)")

followUps:
The transactional outbox writes the event into a table in the same database transaction as the business change, and a separate relay publishes it to the message broker afterwards.

BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=7;
INSERT INTO outbox(id, topic, payload) VALUES(...);
COMMIT;   -- relay later reads outbox, publishes, marks sent

This avoids the dual-write problem: if you update the database and then publish, a crash between the two loses the event. The relay may publish twice after a crash, so consumers must be idempotent. The relay can poll the table or tail the database log (CDC, such as Debezium).

Keep dedupe records at least as long as a duplicate can still arrive, which is the longest of the broker retention, the producer retry window and the replay window, plus a safety margin.

For example, if Kafka keeps messages for 7 days and you may replay a topic, keep ids 7 to 14 days, then purge them with a TTL or a scheduled delete to stop the table growing forever. A dedupe table with 10 million events a day and 14 days holds 140 million ids; at about 40 bytes each that is about 5.6 GB, which is fine.

For naturally idempotent operations such as set-to-value, you need no dedupe table at all.

You find out who uses v1 by logging the version on every request and counting calls per API key per version.

Tag each request with its version (from the URL or header) in your logs and metrics, then query: version=v1 grouped by client id, last 30 days. Build a dashboard and a list of top v1 callers. Then email those owners, add Deprecation and Sunset headers on v1 responses, and run brownouts (short planned failures) a few weeks before shutdown to reveal forgotten clients. Retire v1 only when traffic is near zero or the promised date has passed.

Yes, usually: adding a new enum value can break clients, and changing or removing one almost always does.

Clients often use a switch with a closed list. If your API starts returning status: "REFUNDED_PARTIAL" and an old client's code throws on unknown values, that is a break. Removing or renaming "PENDING" to "WAITING" breaks every client that checks for it.

Mitigations: document from day one that clients must tolerate unknown values, add new values only behind a version or opt-in flag, and for protobuf keep a default UNKNOWN = 0 value.

Return 503 when the problem is on your side and the whole service cannot handle requests, not when one client sent too many.

Examples: an overloaded or dependency-down server shedding load for everyone, or planned maintenance. Include Retry-After there too. 429 says "you specifically are too fast, slow down"; 503 says "we are unavailable, try again later". Clients and monitoring treat them differently: a 429 triggers client-side backoff, while many 503s should page your on-call engineer. So per-client limit hit: 429; global load shedding: 503.

Quota exhaustion should use 429 with a clear error body when it will reset on its own, and 403 only when access is denied by plan or permission and waiting does not help.

A monthly quota of 10,000 calls that is used up: 429 with Retry-After set to the seconds until the reset (or the reset date in the body) lets clients stop and resume. A free plan calling a paid-only endpoint, or an expired subscription: 403 (or 402), as waiting will not fix it. Always put the reason in the structured error body so developers do not have to guess.

You limit by output tokens by reserving an estimate first and settling the real cost afterwards.

  1. Before the call, deduct a worst-case reservation, for example max_tokens plus the known input tokens.
  2. While streaming, count tokens as they are emitted, and cut the stream if the budget is hit.
  3. At the end, refund the difference between reservation and actual use.

Example: bucket has 10,000 tokens; request has 500 input and max_tokens 2,000, so reserve 2,500; the model uses 800 output, so refund 1,200. A bucket may briefly go slightly negative, so the next request waits.

You protect a tool API by never trusting the agent's request as the user's intent: enforce permissions on the server and treat every call as potentially hostile.

  • Authorize with the end user's scoped, short-lived token, not a powerful shared key.
  • Use least privilege: read-only tools by default, and a human confirmation step for destructive or money-moving actions.
  • Validate every argument against a schema and limits (amounts, recipients, row counts).
  • Rate-limit and budget per agent session, and log each call so abuse can be traced.

Injected text can make the model ask for anything, so the API has to be safe even if the model is fully compromised.
